claim: SIRT2 is expressed in the heart at relatively high levels.
source: We first showed that SIRT2 is expressed in the heart (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and in H9c2 cardiomyoblasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) at relatively high levels.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and 1B demonstrating SIRT2 protein expression in heart tissue and H9c2 cells.

claim: SIRT2 expression is higher in mouse hearts 4 weeks after TAC compared to sham.
source: We also found that SIRT2 expression was higher in the hearts of mice 4 weeks after TAC compared to sham (Figure 1A), while the levels of other sirtuin family members with major deacetylation activity that have been studied in the heart (i.e., SIRT1, SIRT3, and SIRT6) were not different.
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 1A showing increased SIRT2 protein levels in TAC versus sham hearts.

claim: The levels of SIRT1, SIRT3, and SIRT6 are not different in mouse hearts 4 weeks after TAC compared to sham.
source: We also found that SIRT2 expression was higher in the hearts of mice 4 weeks after TAC compared to sham (Figure 1A), while the levels of other sirtuin family members with major deacetylation activity that have been studied in the heart (i.e., SIRT1, SIRT3, and SIRT6) were not different.
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 1A showing no significant changes in SIRT1, SIRT3, and SIRT6 protein levels between TAC and sham groups.

claim: SIRT2 levels are significantly increased in explanted hearts from end-stage heart failure patients with dilated cardiomyopathy.
source: Additionally, we noted a significant increase in the levels of SIRT2 in the explanted hearts from end-stage HF patients with dilated cardiomyopathy (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 1B showing increased SIRT2 protein levels in human heart failure samples compared to non-failing controls.

claim: SIRT2 is increased in explanted hearts from patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy.
source: We also assessed the levels of SIRT2 in explanted hearts from patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy and showed that SIRT2 is increased in these hearts (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 1C showing increased SIRT2 protein levels in ischemic cardiomyopathy samples compared to non-failing controls.

claim: SIRT2 levels are increased in heart failure and ischemic injury.
source: These results indicate that SIRT2 levels are increased in HF and ischemic injury.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing increased SIRT2 in TAC, dilated cardiomyopathy, and ischemic cardiomyopathy models.

claim: Sirt2-/- hearts display no change in other sirtuin family members at the mRNA level.
source: We assessed whether Sirt2 deletion affects the levels of other sirtuin family members in the heart. Sirt2-/- hearts displayed no change in other sirtuin family members at the mRNA level, and no change in protein levels of SIRT1, SIRT3, or SIRT6 (sirtuins with major deacetylation activity) was detected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing no significant changes in Sirt1, Sirt3, Sirt4, Sirt5, Sirt6, and Sirt7 mRNA levels.

claim: Sirt2-/- hearts display no change in protein levels of SIRT1, SIRT3, or SIRT6.
source: We assessed whether Sirt2 deletion affects the levels of other sirtuin family members in the heart. Sirt2-/- hearts displayed no change in other sirtuin family members at the mRNA level, and no change in protein levels of SIRT1, SIRT3, or SIRT6 (sirtuins with major deacetylation activity) was detected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing no significant changes in SIRT1, SIRT3, and SIRT6 protein levels between WT and Sirt2-/- hearts.

claim: Sirt2-/- mice display normal cardiovascular parameters at baseline and no overt phenotype.
source: Sirt2-/- mice displayed normal cardiovascular parameters at baseline and no overt phenotype.
evidence: Based on observation of the mice, though specific baseline measurements are not shown in detail.

claim: Sirt2-/- mice display improved cardiac function after TAC compared to littermate controls, as assessed by fractional shortening and ejection fraction.
source: However, in response to TAC, Sirt2-/- mice displayed improved cardiac function than littermate controls, as assessed by fractional shortening (FS) and ejection fraction (EF) (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data in Figure 2A and B showing significantly higher EF and FS in Sirt2-/- mice after TAC.

claim: Sirt2-/- mice display evidence of less cardiac hypertrophy after TAC, as evidenced by lower interventricular septal thickness on echocardiography.
source: Additionally, Sirt2-/- mice displayed evidence of less cardiac hypertrophy, as evidenced by lower interventricular septal (IVS) thickness on echocardiography (Figure 2C), and reduced cardiac size and heart weight to body weight ratio on gross examination (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data in Figure 2C showing lower IVS thickness in Sirt2-/- mice after TAC.

claim: Sirt2-/- mice display reduced cardiac size and heart weight to body weight ratio after TAC on gross examination.
source: Additionally, Sirt2-/- mice displayed evidence of less cardiac hypertrophy, as evidenced by lower interventricular septal (IVS) thickness on echocardiography (Figure 2C), and reduced cardiac size and heart weight to body weight ratio on gross examination (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by gross heart images and HW/BW measurements in Figure 2D and E showing smaller hearts and lower HW/BW ratio in Sirt2-/- mice after TAC.

claim: Sirt2-/- hearts show smaller cardiomyocytes after pressure overload, as assessed by H&E staining.
source: Histological examination of the hearts also showed smaller cardiomyocytes in Sirt2-/- hearts after PO, as assessed by H&E staining (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: Supported by histological data in Figure 2F and G showing reduced cross-sectional area of cardiomyocytes in Sirt2-/- hearts after TAC.

claim: Deletion of Sirt2 results in protection of the heart against pressure overload with improved cardiac function and less cardiac hypertrophy.
source: These data indicate that deletion of Sirt2 results in protection of the heart against PO with improved cardiac function and less cardiac hypertrophy.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing improved cardiac function and reduced hypertrophy in Sirt2-/- mice after TAC.

claim: Ejection fraction and fractional shortening are significantly higher in Sirt2-/- mice compared to controls at 7 days after I/R.
source: We subjected Sirt2-/- and their littermate wild-type (WT) controls to I/R and cardiac function was assessed after 7 and 21 days. At both time points, EF and FS were significantly higher in Sirt2-/- mice compared to controls (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data in Figure 3A showing significantly higher EF and FS in Sirt2-/- mice at 7 days post-I/R.

claim: Ejection fraction and fractional shortening are significantly higher in Sirt2-/- mice compared to controls at 21 days after I/R.
source: We subjected Sirt2-/- and their littermate wild-type (WT) controls to I/R and cardiac function was assessed after 7 and 21 days. At both time points, EF and FS were significantly higher in Sirt2-/- mice compared to controls (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data in Figure 3B showing significantly higher EF and FS in Sirt2-/- mice at 21 days post-I/R.

claim: Fractional shortening was comparable between WT and Sirt2-/- mice on day 3 after I/R, but quickly deteriorated in WT mice while Sirt2-/- mice maintained their cardiac function.
source: Time course of cardiac assessment showed that while FS was comparable between WT and Sirt2-/- on day 3, it quickly deteriorated in WT mice, consistent with transition into HF, while Sirt2-/- mice maintained their cardiac function (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by time course data in Figure 3C showing divergence in FS between WT and Sirt2-/- mice after day 3 post-I/R.

claim: Neonatal rat cardiomyocytes with Sirt2 knockdown display improved cell viability in response to H2O2.
source: To further support these findings, we assessed the effects of Sirt2 modulation on cell death in response to H2O2 in neonatal rat cardiomyocytes (NRCMs) treated with control or Sirt2 siRNA by measuring propidium iodide (PI) positive cells. We found that cells with Sirt2 knockdown (KD) displayed improved cell viability in response to H2O2 (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by PI staining data in Figure 3D and E showing reduced cell death in Sirt2 siRNA-treated NRCMs exposed to H2O2.

claim: SIRT2 exerts detrimental effects in the heart in response to pressure overload and ischemia-reperfusion, and its deletion leads to protective effects.
source: Overall, these results indicate that SIRT2 exerts detrimental effects in the heart in response to PO and I/R, and that its deletion leads to protective effects.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing improved outcomes in Sirt2-/- mice after TAC and I/R.

claim: cs-Sirt2-/- mice display improved cardiac function compared to WT controls at 1 week after TAC.
source: The cs-Sirt2-/- mice were then subjected to TAC with littermate Cre negative mice as control, and cardiac functions (EF and FS) were assessed at 1 and 2 weeks after injury. At both time points, cs-Sirt2-/- mice displayed improved cardiac function compared to WT controls (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data in Figure 4A showing significantly higher EF and FS in cs-Sirt2-/- mice at 7 days post-TAC.

claim: cs-Sirt2-/- mice display improved cardiac function compared to WT controls at 2 weeks after TAC.
source: The cs-Sirt2-/- mice were then subjected to TAC with littermate Cre negative mice as control, and cardiac functions (EF and FS) were assessed at 1 and 2 weeks after injury. At both time points, cs-Sirt2-/- mice displayed improved cardiac function compared to WT controls (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data in Figure 4B showing significantly higher EF and FS in cs-Sirt2-/- mice at 14 days post-TAC.

claim: Heart failure markers Nppa and Nppb are significantly lower in cs-Sirt2-/- mice after TAC.
source: Consistent with these data, HF markers in the heart, including Nppa and Nppb, were significantly lower in cs-Sirt2-/- mice after TAC (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4C and D showing reduced mRNA levels of Nppa and Nppb in cs-Sirt2-/- hearts after TAC.

claim: Female cs-Sirt2-/- mice are protected against TAC at 7 and 14 days.
source: To determine whether these effects are gender specific, we also preformed TAC in female Sirt2f/f and cs-Sirt2-/- mice and demonstrated that they are also protected against TAC at 7 and 14 days (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 showing improved EF and FS in female cs-Sirt2-/- mice after TAC.

claim: The hearts of cs-Sirt2-/- mice are protected against I/R, with significantly higher cardiac function 14 days after I/R.
source: Finally, the hearts of cs-Sirt2-/- mice are also protected against I/R, as their function was significantly higher (Figure 4E) and degree of ischemic damage was lower (Figure 4F) than Sirt2f/f mice 14 days after I/R.
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data in Figure 4E showing higher EF and FS in cs-Sirt2-/- mice at 7 and 14 days post-I/R.

claim: The degree of ischemic damage is lower in cs-Sirt2-/- mice compared to Sirt2f/f mice 14 days after I/R.
source: Finally, the hearts of cs-Sirt2-/- mice are also protected against I/R, as their function was significantly higher (Figure 4E) and degree of ischemic damage was lower (Figure 4F) than Sirt2f/f mice 14 days after I/R.
evidence: Supported by necrotic area measurements in Figure 4F showing reduced ischemic damage in cs-Sirt2-/- mice.

claim: SIRT2 deacetylates NRF2 protein in the liver and alters iron release from hepatocytes.
source: We previously showed that SIRT2 deacetylates NRF2 protein in the liver and alters iron release from hepatocytes (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Deacetylation of NRF2 leads to protein destabilization.
source: Since deacetylation of NRF2 leads to protein destabilization and NRF2 regulates the expression of many antioxidant genes, we hypothesized that the mechanism for the protective effects of Sirt2 deletion in response to stress is through decreased NRF2 deacetylation and degradation, resulting in increased expression of antioxidant proteins.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about NRF2 regulation and previous findings.

claim: NRF2 regulates the expression of many antioxidant genes.
source: Since deacetylation of NRF2 leads to protein destabilization and NRF2 regulates the expression of many antioxidant genes, we hypothesized that the mechanism for the protective effects of Sirt2 deletion in response to stress is through decreased NRF2 deacetylation and degradation, resulting in increased expression of antioxidant proteins.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about NRF2 function as a transcription factor for antioxidant genes.

claim: SIRT2 interacts with NRF2 in the heart of WT mice.
source: To test this hypothesis, we first assessed whether there is physical interaction between SIRT2 and NRF2 in the heart. Co-immunoprecipitation (IP) experiments showed that SIRT2 interacts with NRF2 in the heart of WT mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5A showing SIRT2 and NRF2 co-precipitate in heart extracts.

claim: NRF2 acetylation levels are increased in Sirt2-/- hearts.
source: We then measured acetylation levels of NRF2 in WT and Sirt2-/- hearts, and showed that NRF2 acetylation levels are increased within Sirt2-/- hearts (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5B showing increased acetylated NRF2 in Sirt2-/- hearts.

claim: Treatment of NRCMs with Sirt2 siRNA results in increased NRF2 protein levels compared with control siRNA.
source: We then assessed whether deacetylation of NRF2 alters its levels in the cardiac cells, as shown before in the liver (Yang et al., 2017). Treatment of NRCMs with Sirt2 siRNA resulted in increased NRF2 protein levels compared with control siRNA, indicating that SIRT2 leads to a reduction in the levels of NRF2 protein (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 5C showing increased NRF2 protein in Sirt2 siRNA-treated NRCMs.

claim: SIRT2 leads to a reduction in the levels of NRF2 protein.
source: Treatment of NRCMs with Sirt2 siRNA resulted in increased NRF2 protein levels compared with control siRNA, indicating that SIRT2 leads to a reduction in the levels of NRF2 protein (Figure 5C).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Sirt2 knockdown increases NRF2 protein levels.

claim: NRF2 protein levels are significantly lower starting at 60 min after treatment with cycloheximide in cells treated with control siRNA, leading to almost complete degradation at 120 min.
source: Since NRF2 protein levels are higher in Sirt2-/- hearts, we next assessed whether SIRT2 alters the stability of NRF2 protein. NRF2 levels were significantly lower starting at 60 min after treatment with the protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX), leading to almost complete degradation at 120 min in cells treated with control siRNA. However, we noted no change in NRF2 protein levels in cells treated with Sirt2 siRNA (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by protein stability assay data in Figure 5D showing time-dependent degradation of NRF2 in control siRNA-treated cells.

claim: No change in NRF2 protein levels is observed in cells treated with Sirt2 siRNA after cycloheximide treatment.
source: NRF2 levels were significantly lower starting at 60 min after treatment with the protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX), leading to almost complete degradation at 120 min in cells treated with control siRNA. However, we noted no change in NRF2 protein levels in cells treated with Sirt2 siRNA (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by protein stability assay data in Figure 5D showing stable NRF2 protein levels in Sirt2 siRNA-treated cells after CHX treatment.

claim: SIRT2 binds to NRF2, and its deacetylation leads to the instability and degradation of NRF2.
source: These data indicate that SIRT2 binds to NRF2, and its deacetylation leads to the instability and degradation of NRF2.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing SIRT2-NRF2 interaction, increased NRF2 acetylation in Sirt2-/- hearts, and increased NRF2 stability with Sirt2 knockdown.

claim: NRF2 is a transcription factor and upon activation, translocates into the nucleus to exert its transcriptional activity.
source: NRF2 is a transcription factor and upon activation, translocates into the nucleus to exert its transcriptional activity (Hybertson et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to established knowledge about NRF2 function.

claim: Nuclear level of NRF2 is increased in NRCMs with Sirt2 knockdown.
source: Thus, we measured nuclear level of NRF2 and found it to be increased in NRCMs with Sirt2 KD (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by nuclear fractionation data in Figure 5E showing increased nuclear NRF2 in Sirt2 siRNA-treated NRCMs.

claim: SIRT2 overexpression in H9c2 cells results in lower levels of known NRF2 target genes.
source: Since the increase in nuclear levels of NRF2 suggests possibly higher transcriptional activity of the protein, we next assessed the effects of Sirt2 modulation on NRF2 transcriptional activity in H9c2 cells treated with lentivirus expressing either control or SIRT2 lentivirus. Consistent with its increased nuclear levels, SIRT2 overexpression in H9c2 cells resulted in lower levels of known NRF2 target genes (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5F-H showing reduced expression of NRF2 target genes in SIRT2-overexpressing H9c2 cells.

claim: The mRNA levels of non-NRF2 targeted antioxidant genes are not affected by SIRT2 overexpression.
source: However, the mRNA levels of non-NRF2 targeted antioxidant genes were not affected by SIRT2 overexpression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing no significant changes in Cat, Sod1, Sod2, and Sod3 expression with SIRT2 overexpression.

claim: NRF2 protein increases with Sirt2 knockdown in mouse HL-1 atrial cell line.
source: We confirmed the data in mouse HL-1 atrial cell line and showed an increase in NRF2 protein with Sirt2 KD and a decrease in NRF2 target proteins with overexpression of SIRT2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A showing increased NRF2 protein in Sirt2 siRNA-treated HL-1 cells.

claim: NRF2 target proteins decrease with overexpression of SIRT2 in mouse HL-1 atrial cell line.
source: We confirmed the data in mouse HL-1 atrial cell line and showed an increase in NRF2 protein with Sirt2 KD and a decrease in NRF2 target proteins with overexpression of SIRT2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B-D showing reduced expression of NRF2 target genes in SIRT2-overexpressing HL-1 cells.

claim: NRCMs treated with Sirt2 siRNA display less ROS levels after treatment with H2O2.
source: Since our data suggest a role for SIRT2 in the regulation of NRF2-mediated expression of antioxidant genes, we next assessed whether SIRT2 has an effect on reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. NRCMs treated with Sirt2 siRNA displayed less ROS levels after treatment with H2O2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), further supporting a role for SIRT2 in regulating oxidative state of cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Supported by DHE fluorescence data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 showing reduced ROS in Sirt2 siRNA-treated NRCMs exposed to H2O2.

claim: SIRT2 has a role in regulating oxidative state of cardiomyocytes.
source: NRCMs treated with Sirt2 siRNA displayed less ROS levels after treatment with H2O2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), further supporting a role for SIRT2 in regulating oxidative state of cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Sirt2 knockdown reduces ROS levels in cardiomyocytes.

claim: Sirt2/Nrf2 double KO mice display reduced EF and FS compared to Sirt2-/- mice after I/R injury.
source: To determine whether the protective effects of SIRT2 are mediated through NRF2, we generated Sirt2/Nrf2 double KO mice and subjected the mice to I/R injury. The Sirt2/Nrf2 double KO mice displayed reduced EF and FS compared to Sirt2-/- mice (Figure 6A and B), indicating that deletion of Nrf2 reverses the protective effects of SIRT2.
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data in Figure 6A and B showing lower EF and FS in Sirt2-/-/Nrf2-/- mice compared to Sirt2-/- mice after I/R.

claim: Deletion of Nrf2 reverses the protective effects of SIRT2 deletion.
source: The Sirt2/Nrf2 double KO mice displayed reduced EF and FS compared to Sirt2-/- mice (Figure 6A and B), indicating that deletion of Nrf2 reverses the protective effects of SIRT2.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Sirt2-/-/Nrf2-/- mice lose the cardiac protection seen in Sirt2-/- mice.

claim: Treatment with AGK2 did not change the systolic function of the heart, as assessed by EF and FS.
source: At the conclusion of the study, their cardiac function and heart chamber size were assessed using echocardiography (Figure 6C). Treatment with AGK2 did not change the systolic function of the heart, as assessed by EF, FS (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data in Figure 6E and F showing no significant difference in EF and FS between vehicle and AGK2-treated mice after TAC.

claim: Measures of cardiac size, as assessed by left ventricular diameter during diastole and systole, were increased in AGK2-treated mice after TAC.
source: However, measures of cardiac size, as assessed by left ventricular (LV) diameter during diastole and systole (LVDd and LVDs, respectively), were increased, while measures of LV wall diameter, as assessed by IVSd and posterior wall thickness during diastole (PWTd), were reduced (Figure 6G–J).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data in Figure 6G and H showing increased LVDd and LVDs in AGK2-treated mice after TAC.

claim: Measures of LV wall diameter, as assessed by IVSd and posterior wall thickness during diastole, were reduced in AGK2-treated mice after TAC.
source: However, measures of cardiac size, as assessed by left ventricular (LV) diameter during diastole and systole (LVDd and LVDs, respectively), were increased, while measures of LV wall diameter, as assessed by IVSd and posterior wall thickness during diastole (PWTd), were reduced (Figure 6G–J).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data in Figure 6I and J showing reduced IVSd and PWTd in AGK2-treated mice after TAC.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of SIRT2 can protect the heart against cardiac hypertrophy and improve cardiac remodeling in response to pressure overload.
source: These results indicate that pharmacological inhibition of SIRT2 can protect the heart against cardiac hypertrophy and improve cardiac remodeling in response to PO.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing reduced cardiac wall thickness and improved chamber dimensions in AGK2-treated mice after TAC.

claim: Sirtuins play a major role in post-translational modification of proteins.
source: Sirtuins play a major role in post-translational modification of proteins, and their deletion have been shown to lead to a number of physiological changes and pathological conditions (Baur et al., 2012; Watroba and Szukiewicz, 2021; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on sirtuin function.

claim: Deletion of sirtuins has been shown to lead to a number of physiological changes and pathological conditions.
source: Sirtuins play a major role in post-translational modification of proteins, and their deletion have been shown to lead to a number of physiological changes and pathological conditions (Baur et al., 2012; Watroba and Szukiewicz, 2021; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on sirtuin function.

claim: SIRT2 has detrimental effects in the heart in the setting of cardiac insults.
source: In this paper, we used genetic models to show that SIRT2 has detrimental effects in the heart in the setting of cardiac insults and demonstrate that the deleterious effects of SIRT2 is through increased NRF2 deacetylation and its degradation and eventual reduction in the levels of antioxidant genes.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing improved cardiac outcomes with Sirt2 deletion in TAC and I/R models.

claim: The deleterious effects of SIRT2 are through increased NRF2 deacetylation and its degradation and eventual reduction in the levels of antioxidant genes.
source: In this paper, we used genetic models to show that SIRT2 has detrimental effects in the heart in the setting of cardiac insults and demonstrate that the deleterious effects of SIRT2 is through increased NRF2 deacetylation and its degradation and eventual reduction in the levels of antioxidant genes.
evidence: Inferred from the mechanistic data showing SIRT2 deacetylates NRF2, leading to its degradation and reduced antioxidant gene expression.

claim: Treatment of mice with AGK2, a selective SIRT2 inhibitor, results in protection against cardiac hypertrophy in response to pressure overload.
source: Finally, we provide a clinical significance for our findings and show that treatment of mice with AGK2, a selective SIRT2 inhibitor, results in protection against cardiac hypertrophy in response to PO.
evidence: Supported by data showing reduced cardiac wall thickness in AGK2-treated mice after TAC.

claim: NRF2 plays a major role in the regulation of genes involved in oxidative stress, metabolic processes, drug metabolism, and stress response.
source: NRF2 plays a major role in the regulation of genes involved in oxidative stress, metabolic processes, drug metabolism, and stress response, among others.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about NRF2 function.

claim: Direct activation of NRF2 may have unwanted side effects.
source: Thus, its activation has been studied extensively in a number of diseases, however, these studies have not led to an effective therapy. It is possible that direct activation of NRF2 may have unwanted side effects.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the lack of effective NRF2-based therapies.

claim: Targeting SIRT2 and indirect activation of NRF2 by altering its post-translational protein modification may prove to be a more effective therapeutic strategy for a number of diseases.
source: Our studies provide a proof of concept that targeting SIRT2 and indirect activation of NRF2 by altering its post-translational protein modification may prove to be a more effective therapeutic strategy for a number of diseases.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the study findings showing protective effects of SIRT2 inhibition.

claim: Cardiac hypertrophy is a major complication of hypertrophy and metabolic disorders.
source: Cardiac hypertrophy is a major complication of hypertrophy and metabolic disorders in this country (Husser et al., 2018; Moon et al., 2020; Semsarian et al., 2015), however, our treatment options are limited.
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on cardiac hypertrophy.

claim: Treatment options for cardiac hypertrophy are limited.
source: Cardiac hypertrophy is a major complication of hypertrophy and metabolic disorders in this country (Husser et al., 2018; Moon et al., 2020; Semsarian et al., 2015), however, our treatment options are limited.
evidence: Based on established clinical knowledge about cardiac hypertrophy treatment.

claim: Targeting SIRT2 with AGK2 would improve cardiac remodeling and cardiac hypertrophy in response to pressure overload.
source: Our data indicate that targeting SIRT2 with AGK2 would improve cardiac remodeling and cardiac hypertrophy in response to PO, potentially providing a novel therapy for these disorders.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing improved cardiac parameters in AGK2-treated mice after TAC.

claim: Systemic inhibition of SIRT2 may have unwanted side effects.
source: However, systemic inhibition of SIRT2 may have unwanted side effects, which would need to be investigated further.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about potential limitations of systemic SIRT2 inhibition.

claim: The systemic and cardiac-independent effects of AGK drug cannot be ruled out in the studies.
source: Additionally, the systemic and cardiac-independent effects of AGK drug cannot be ruled out in our studies.
evidence: Acknowledgment of study limitation regarding potential off-target effects of AGK2.

claim: The data are not consistent with two previous studies that have shown protective effects of SIRT2 in the heart.
source: Finally, our data are not consistent with two previous studies that have shown protective effects of SIRT2 in the heart, with one study showing that deletion of Sirt2 increases age-related and angiotensin II-mediated cardiac hypertrophy (Tang et al., 2017), while another study showing that Sirt2 deficiency leads to cardiac dysfunction and cardiac hypertrophy (Sarikhani et al., 2018).
evidence: Comparison with previously published studies showing contradictory results.

claim: Deletion of Sirt2 increases age-related and angiotensin II-mediated cardiac hypertrophy according to Tang et al., 2017.
source: Finally, our data are not consistent with two previous studies that have shown protective effects of SIRT2 in the heart, with one study showing that deletion of Sirt2 increases age-related and angiotensin II-mediated cardiac hypertrophy (Tang et al., 2017), while another study showing that Sirt2 deficiency leads to cardiac dysfunction and cardiac hypertrophy (Sarikhani et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tang et al., 2017.

claim: Sirt2 deficiency leads to cardiac dysfunction and cardiac hypertrophy according to Sarikhani et al., 2018.
source: Finally, our data are not consistent with two previous studies that have shown protective effects of SIRT2 in the heart, with one study showing that deletion of Sirt2 increases age-related and angiotensin II-mediated cardiac hypertrophy (Tang et al., 2017), while another study showing that Sirt2 deficiency leads to cardiac dysfunction and cardiac hypertrophy (Sarikhani et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sarikhani et al., 2018.

claim: The genetic background of the mice and the different gene targeting strategy might have contributed to the difference in results between studies.
source: The reason for this discrepancy in our data is not clear, however, we used both global and cardiac specific KO of Sirt2, while these studies have used mice with global deletion of the gene. The genetic background of the mice and the different gene targeting strategy might have also contributed to the difference.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about potential sources of discrepancy between studies.

claim: SIRT2 demonstrates detrimental effects in the heart through its regulation of antioxidant proteins by NRF2 protein.
source: However, we used two different genetic models (global and cardiac specific KO of Sirt2) and a pharmacological approach to test our hypothesis, all of which produced similar results. Finally, we provide a mechanism for the deleterious effects of SIRT2 in the heart through its regulation of antioxidant proteins by NRF2 protein.
evidence: Inferred from the combined mechanistic data showing SIRT2 regulates NRF2 and antioxidant gene expression.

claim: SIRT2 binds to NRF2 and Sirt2 deletion leads to an increase in NRF2 stability and nuclear levels, resulting in higher production of antioxidant genes.
source: In summary, our data demonstrate that SIRT2 has deleterious effects in the heart through its post-translational modification of NRF2. We show that SIRT2 binds to NRF2 and that Sirt2 deletion leads to an increase in NRF2 stability and nuclear levels, resulting in higher production of antioxidant genes.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing SIRT2-NRF2 interaction, increased NRF2 stability and nuclear localization with Sirt2 deletion, and increased antioxidant gene expression.

claim: AGK2 is a specific inhibitor of SIRT2.
source: Finally, our results provide a potential therapy for cardiac hypertrophy by using AGK2, a specific inhibitor of SIRT2.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about AGK2 and citations to previous studies characterizing AGK2 as a SIRT2 inhibitor (He et al., 2012; Outeiro et al., 2007; Petrilli et al., 2013).

claim: Sirtuin family of proteins comprise class III of histone deacetylases.
source: Sirtuin (SIRT) family of proteins comprise class III of histone deacetylases.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about sirtuin classification.

claim: SIRTs require NAD+ to carry out their enzymatic reaction.
source: SIRTs require NAD+ to carry out their enzymatic reaction, and have been implicated in a wide range of cellular processes including aging, apoptosis, response to stress and inflammation, control of energy efficiency, circadian clocks, and mitochondrial biogenesis (Baur et al., 2012; Preyat and Leo, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on sirtuin function.

claim: SIRTs have been implicated in a wide range of cellular processes including aging, apoptosis, response to stress and inflammation, control of energy efficiency, circadian clocks, and mitochondrial biogenesis.
source: SIRTs require NAD+ to carry out their enzymatic reaction, and have been implicated in a wide range of cellular processes including aging, apoptosis, response to stress and inflammation, control of energy efficiency, circadian clocks, and mitochondrial biogenesis (Baur et al., 2012; Preyat and Leo, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on sirtuin function.

claim: Seven sirtuins (SIRT1-7) have been identified in mammals.
source: In mammals, seven sirtuins (SIRT1-7) have been identified, which are categorized according to their subcellular localization to the nucleus (SIRT1, -6, and -7), mitochondria (SIRT3, -4, and -5), and cytoplasm (SIRT2).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about mammalian sirtuins.

claim: Sirtuins are categorized according to their subcellular localization to the nucleus (SIRT1, -6, and -7), mitochondria (SIRT3, -4, and -5), and cytoplasm (SIRT2).
source: In mammals, seven sirtuins (SIRT1-7) have been identified, which are categorized according to their subcellular localization to the nucleus (SIRT1, -6, and -7), mitochondria (SIRT3, -4, and -5), and cytoplasm (SIRT2).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about sirtuin subcellular localization.

claim: SIRT1–3 have a robust deacetylation activity.
source: SIRT1–3 have a robust deacetylation activity, while SIRT4 is reported to display ADP-ribosyltransferase activity.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about sirtuin enzymatic activities.

claim: SIRT4 is reported to display ADP-ribosyltransferase activity.
source: SIRT1–3 have a robust deacetylation activity, while SIRT4 is reported to display ADP-ribosyltransferase activity.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about SIRT4 enzymatic activity.

claim: SIRT5 may function as a protein desuccinylase and demalonylase.
source: SIRT5 may function as a protein desuccinylase and demalonylase, and SIRT6 and SIRT7 display weak deacetylase activity (Du et al., 2011; Haigis et al., 2006; Michishita et al., 2005; Pan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on SIRT5 function.

claim: SIRT6 and SIRT7 display weak deacetylase activity.
source: SIRT5 may function as a protein desuccinylase and demalonylase, and SIRT6 and SIRT7 display weak deacetylase activity (Du et al., 2011; Haigis et al., 2006; Michishita et al., 2005; Pan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on SIRT6 and SIRT7 function.

claim: The effects of SIRT1 in the heart are complex.
source: A number of SIRTs have been studied in the heart (for review, please see Matsushima and Sadoshima, 2015). The effects of SIRT1 in the heart are complex.
evidence: Supported by citation to review article and subsequent description of context-dependent SIRT1 effects.

claim: Sirt1 deletion protects against pressure overload-induced cardiac hypertrophy.
source: Sirt1 deletion protects against pressure overload (PO)-induced cardiac hypertrophy (Oka et al., 2011; Sundaresan et al., 2011); however, low-level overexpression of SIRT1 in the heart attenuates age-associated cardiac hypertrophy, fibrosis, and cardiac dysfunction, while high-level overexpression of SIRT1 increases these pathological effects (Alcendor et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Oka et al., 2011 and Sundaresan et al., 2011.

claim: Low-level overexpression of SIRT1 in the heart attenuates age-associated cardiac hypertrophy, fibrosis, and cardiac dysfunction.
source: Sirt1 deletion protects against pressure overload (PO)-induced cardiac hypertrophy (Oka et al., 2011; Sundaresan et al., 2011); however, low-level overexpression of SIRT1 in the heart attenuates age-associated cardiac hypertrophy, fibrosis, and cardiac dysfunction, while high-level overexpression of SIRT1 increases these pathological effects (Alcendor et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alcendor et al., 2007.

claim: High-level overexpression of SIRT1 increases age-associated cardiac hypertrophy, fibrosis, and cardiac dysfunction.
source: Sirt1 deletion protects against pressure overload (PO)-induced cardiac hypertrophy (Oka et al., 2011; Sundaresan et al., 2011); however, low-level overexpression of SIRT1 in the heart attenuates age-associated cardiac hypertrophy, fibrosis, and cardiac dysfunction, while high-level overexpression of SIRT1 increases these pathological effects (Alcendor et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alcendor et al., 2007.

claim: SIRT1 exerts protective effects in the setting of ischemia-reperfusion.
source: In the setting of ischemia-reperfusion (I/R), SIRT1 exerts protective effects: Sirt1 knockout (KO) in the heart increases I/R-induced injury, while its overexpression protects against I/R-induced injury (Hsu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hsu et al., 2010.

claim: Sirt1 knockout in the heart increases I/R-induced injury.
source: In the setting of ischemia-reperfusion (I/R), SIRT1 exerts protective effects: Sirt1 knockout (KO) in the heart increases I/R-induced injury, while its overexpression protects against I/R-induced injury (Hsu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hsu et al., 2010.

claim: SIRT1 overexpression protects against I/R-induced injury.
source: In the setting of ischemia-reperfusion (I/R), SIRT1 exerts protective effects: Sirt1 knockout (KO) in the heart increases I/R-induced injury, while its overexpression protects against I/R-induced injury (Hsu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hsu et al., 2010.

claim: The effects of SIRT1 on cardiac response to stress are dependent on its expression levels as well as the context of injury.
source: Thus, it appears that the effects of SIRT1 on cardiac response to stress are dependent on its expression levels as well as the context of injury.
evidence: Inferred from the cited studies showing different effects of SIRT1 depending on expression level and type of cardiac stress.

claim: SIRT3 protects against both cardiac hypertrophy and I/R injury.
source: SIRT3 has also been studied in the heart and shown to protect against both cardiac hypertrophy and I/R injury (Porter et al., 2014; Sundaresan et al., 2009), while SIRT6 KO mice exhibit cardiac hypertrophy (Sundaresan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Porter et al., 2014 and Sundaresan et al., 2009.

claim: SIRT6 KO mice exhibit cardiac hypertrophy.
source: SIRT3 has also been studied in the heart and shown to protect against both cardiac hypertrophy and I/R injury (Porter et al., 2014; Sundaresan et al., 2009), while SIRT6 KO mice exhibit cardiac hypertrophy (Sundaresan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sundaresan et al., 2012.

claim: Advanced glycation end products and its receptor promote diabetic cardiomyopathy through suppression of SIRT2.
source: One study showed that deletion of Sirt2 reduces AMPK activation and increases age-related and angiotensin II-mediated cardiac hypertrophy (Tang et al., 2017), while another showed that advanced glycation end products and its receptor promote diabetic cardiomyopathy through suppression of SIRT2, however, KO mice were not used for these studies (Yuan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yuan et al., 2015.

claim: Sirt2 deficiency increases nuclear localization of NFATc2 and its transcription activity.
source: Another study showed that Sirt2 deficiency increases nuclear localization of NFATc2 and its transcription activity, and that NFAT inhibition rescues the cardiac dysfunction in mice with Sirt2 deletion (Sarikhani et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sarikhani et al., 2018.

claim: NFAT inhibition rescues the cardiac dysfunction in mice with Sirt2 deletion.
source: Another study showed that Sirt2 deficiency increases nuclear localization of NFATc2 and its transcription activity, and that NFAT inhibition rescues the cardiac dysfunction in mice with Sirt2 deletion (Sarikhani et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sarikhani et al., 2018.

claim: NRF2 is a transcription factor that activates a number of cytoprotective genes, including antioxidative enzymes.
source: Nuclear factor (erythroid-derived 2)-like 2 (NRF2) is a transcription factor that activates a number of cytoprotective genes, including antioxidative enzymes (Tufekci et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tufekci et al., 2011.

claim: Under normal conditions, NRF2 resides in the cytoplasm and is degraded primarily through its interaction with Keap1.
source: Under normal conditions, NRF2 resides in the cytoplasm, and is degraded primarily through its interaction with Keap1 (kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1), which also serves as a bridge between NRF2 and cullin 3-ubiquitination complex (Tufekci et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tufekci et al., 2011.

claim: Keap1 serves as a bridge between NRF2 and cullin 3-ubiquitination complex.
source: Under normal conditions, NRF2 resides in the cytoplasm, and is degraded primarily through its interaction with Keap1 (kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1), which also serves as a bridge between NRF2 and cullin 3-ubiquitination complex (Tufekci et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tufekci et al., 2011.

claim: Under oxidative stress, NRF2 escapes degradation, translocates into the nucleus, and binds to antioxidant response elements in the promoter of a number of genes.
source: Under oxidative stress, NRF2 escapes degradation, translocates into the nucleus, and binds to antioxidant response elements in the promoter of a number of genes (Kaspar et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kaspar et al., 2009.

claim: NRF2 acetylation is decreased with SIRT1 overexpression.
source: NRF2 acetylation is decreased with SIRT1 overexpression (Kawai et al., 2011); however, an association between SIRT1 and NRF2 has not been demonstrated, and the functional consequences of NRF2 deacetylation have not been studied.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kawai et al., 2011.

claim: An association between SIRT1 and NRF2 has not been demonstrated.
source: NRF2 acetylation is decreased with SIRT1 overexpression (Kawai et al., 2011); however, an association between SIRT1 and NRF2 has not been demonstrated, and the functional consequences of NRF2 deacetylation have not been studied.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature at the time of writing.

claim: The functional consequences of NRF2 deacetylation have not been studied.
source: NRF2 acetylation is decreased with SIRT1 overexpression (Kawai et al., 2011); however, an association between SIRT1 and NRF2 has not been demonstrated, and the functional consequences of NRF2 deacetylation have not been studied.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature at the time of writing.

claim: NRF2 KO mice developed cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure after trans-aortic constriction.
source: NRF2 KO mice developed cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure (HF) after trans-aortic constriction (TAC) (Li et al., 2009), indicating the NRF2 is protective against cardiac stress.
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2009.

claim: NRF2 is protective against cardiac stress.
source: NRF2 KO mice developed cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure (HF) after trans-aortic constriction (TAC) (Li et al., 2009), indicating the NRF2 is protective against cardiac stress.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that NRF2 KO mice develop cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure after TAC.

claim: SIRT2 mediates NRF2 deacetylation in liver cells and its translocation in the nucleus to regulate antioxidant genes.
source: We recently showed that SIRT2 mediates NRF2 deacetylation in the liver cells and its translocation in the nucleus to regulate antioxidant genes (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Yang et al., 2017).

claim: SIRT2 plays a detrimental role in the heart in response to injury, in contrast to a previously published report.
source: In this paper, we show that SIRT2 plays a detrimental role in the heart in response to injury, in contrast to a previously published report (Tang et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from the study findings showing protective effects of Sirt2 deletion, which contradicts Tang et al., 2017.

claim: Deletion of Sirt2 is protective through stabilization and increased nuclear translocation of NRF2, leading to increased expression of antioxidant genes.
source: Mechanistically, deletion of Sirt2 is protective through stabilization and increased nuclear translocation of NRF2, leading to increased expression of antioxidant genes.
evidence: Inferred from the mechanistic data showing increased NRF2 stability, nuclear localization, and antioxidant gene expression with Sirt2 deletion.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of SIRT2 protects the heart against the development of cardiac hypertrophy.
source: Finally and most importantly, we show that pharmacological inhibition of SIRT2 protects the heart against the development of cardiac hypertrophy, opening potential treatment for this disorder.
evidence: Supported by data showing reduced cardiac hypertrophy in AGK2-treated mice after TAC.

claim: The hearts of mice with deletion of Sirt2 display improved cardiac function after ischemia-reperfusion and pressure overload.
source: In this paper, we show that the hearts of mice with deletion of Sirt2 (Sirt2-/-) display improved cardiac function after ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) and pressure overload (PO), suggesting that SIRT2 exerts maladaptive effects in the heart in response to stress.
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data showing improved cardiac function in Sirt2-/- mice after I/R and TAC.

claim: SIRT2 exerts maladaptive effects in the heart in response to stress.
source: In this paper, we show that the hearts of mice with deletion of Sirt2 (Sirt2-/-) display improved cardiac function after ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) and pressure overload (PO), suggesting that SIRT2 exerts maladaptive effects in the heart in response to stress.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Sirt2 deletion improves cardiac outcomes after stress.

claim: Similar results were obtained in mice with cardiomyocyte-specific Sirt2 deletion.
source: Similar results were obtained in mice with cardiomyocyte-specific Sirt2 deletion.
evidence: Supported by data showing improved cardiac function in cs-Sirt2-/- mice after TAC and I/R.

claim: SIRT2 modulates cellular levels and activity of NRF2, which results in reduced expression of antioxidant proteins.
source: Mechanistic studies suggest that SIRT2 modulates cellular levels and activity of nuclear factor (erythroid-derived 2)-like 2 (NRF2), which results in reduced expression of antioxidant proteins.
evidence: Inferred from the mechanistic data showing SIRT2 regulates NRF2 protein levels, stability, nuclear localization, and antioxidant gene expression.

claim: Deletion of Nrf2 in the hearts of Sirt2-/- mice reversed protection after pressure overload.
source: Deletion of Nrf2 in the hearts of Sirt2-/- mice reversed protection after PO.
evidence: Supported by data showing reduced cardiac function in Sirt2-/-/Nrf2-/- mice compared to Sirt2-/- mice after I/R.

claim: Treatment of mouse hearts with a specific SIRT2 inhibitor reduced cardiac size and attenuates cardiac hypertrophy in response to pressure overload.
source: Finally, treatment of mouse hearts with a specific SIRT2 inhibitor reduced cardiac size and attenuates cardiac hypertrophy in response to PO.
evidence: Supported by data showing reduced cardiac wall thickness in AGK2-treated mice after TAC.

claim: SIRT2 has detrimental effects in the heart and plays a role in cardiac response to injury and the progression of cardiac hypertrophy, which makes this protein a unique member of the SIRT family.
source: These data indicate that SIRT2 has detrimental effects in the heart and plays a role in cardiac response to injury and the progression of cardiac hypertrophy, which makes this protein a unique member of the SIRT family.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing detrimental effects of SIRT2 in contrast to protective effects of other sirtuins.

claim: The studies provide a novel approach for treatment of cardiac hypertrophy and injury by targeting SIRT2 pharmacologically.
source: Additionally, our studies provide a novel approach for treatment of cardiac hypertrophy and injury by targeting SIRT2 pharmacologically, providing a novel avenue for the treatment of these disorders.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing protective effects of AGK2 treatment in mice after TAC.
